narrative:
The model estimated a 52.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but because it crosses the school’s risk threshold, your application was rejected. This is a statistical estimate, not a judgment that failure is certain.

The most influential factor was your third-year class standing: you are in the second decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. That relatively low third-year rank pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor, and it worked in your favor: at 3.30 it is slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, pushing toward a prediction of passing. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor; at the third decile versus an accepted average around the sixth, it also pushed toward failure, though less strongly than your third-year standing.

To improve your chances, focus on the academic signal weighted most heavily: your later law-school performance. Speak with admissions or academic advising about what caused the low third-year rank and what evidence you can provide of improvement. Consider delaying the bar exam until you have a structured preparation plan, additional practice, and support. If you reapply, you may also strengthen your file with updated grades, a clear explanation of your trajectory, and proof of readiness for bar-level work.
